questions.question: Define mass movement with both essential clauses, and explain the balance of forces on a slope, water's double game, and the main natural and human triggers.
questions.expected_answer: Mass movement, or mass wasting, is the downslope movement of weathered material under the direct pull of gravity, with no transporting agent involved — no river, glacier or wind. Both clauses are essential. A slope is an unfinished arm-wrestle: gravity's downslope component, growing with slope angle, pushes for failure, while friction, the interlocking of grains, dry cohesion and plant roots hold the line. Water plays both sides: a little moisture binds grains together by surface tension, like a briefly dipped rusk holding its shape, but saturation fills the pores and pushes grains apart, adds great weight, and lubricates potential slide surfaces such as the soil-bedrock junction — which is why most disasters follow heavy or prolonged rain. Other triggers: undercutting of the slope's toe by rivers, waves or road cuttings, removing support where it matters most; earthquakes and blasting shaking grains out of interlock; freeze-thaw levering rock off cliffs; and human actions — stripping vegetation, loading slopes with buildings and dumps, leaking water into the ground, and cutting steep unsupported platforms.

questions.question: Describe the six kinds of mass movement on the speed-and-water grid, giving the mechanism and the identifying field evidence or setting for each.
questions.expected_answer: Soil creep is slowest: the entire soil blanket edges downhill at millimetres per year as wetting-drying and heating-cooling cycles lift grains perpendicular to the slope and settle them vertically, slightly downslope; its evidence is leaning fence posts and gravestones, tree trunks curved at the base, terracettes, and soil banked against the upslope side of walls. Solifluction is creep's high-altitude cousin: where the subsoil is frozen, the thawed waterlogged surface layer cannot drain and flows in tongue-shaped lobes over the frozen floor, as on the high Maloti and Drakensberg plateaus. A landslide is a coherent slab failing along a defined surface and sliding as one body, typically after saturation, readily where a cutting exposes strata dipping parallel to the slope. A slump is the rotational case: failure along a curved, spoon-shaped surface, so the block rotates like an ice-cream scoop turning out of the tub, leaving a crescent scar above and a backward-tilted block below — common in thick soils and embankments. A rock fall is free-fall: frost- or heat-levered blocks drop, bounce and shatter into the talus below cliffs. A mud flow is fastest and wettest: debris saturated into a fluid slurry racing down valleys and setting hard, most dangerous on burnt or cleared slopes after cloudbursts. The grid runs creep, solifluction, landslide, slump, rock fall, mud flow — speed rising, water rising with it.

questions.question: Analyse the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal disaster as a mass movement case study, and set out the four families of prevention and minimisation with named measures and South African applications.
questions.expected_answer: In April 2022 a stalled weather system dropped more than 300 millimetres of rain on parts of the Durban metro in 24 hours — several months' rainfall in a day. The saturated, steep coastal hills failed in hundreds of places almost at once: landslides and mud flows swept through formal and informal settlements, more than 400 people died, thousands of homes were destroyed, and roads, rail, the port and water infrastructure suffered billions of rands in damage. The analysis must include unequal risk: losses concentrated where poverty had pushed families onto steep unstable slopes with hand-cut platforms, stripped vegetation, leaking water and no engineering — the rain was general but the danger was not. The Merriespruit tailings disaster of 1994, where a rain-topped tailings dam liquefied into a mud flow that killed seventeen people, shows the same alignment of saturation, slope and settlement. Prevention groups into four families: reshape and reinforce the slope — regrading, terracing, retaining walls and gabions at the toe, rock anchors, mesh and catch fences as used above mountain-pass hairpins; control the water — crest cut-off drains, perforated subsurface drains, sealed cracks, repaired leaks, and no stormwater discharged onto slope faces; protect the surface — preserving and restoring vegetation whose roots bind the soil, re-grassing burnt slopes, controlling grazing; and plan the settlement — GIS hazard maps overlaying slope, soil, drainage and rainfall, zoning housing off red zones, building regulations for cuttings and platforms, rainfall-triggered early warning as Durban has developed since 2022, community education on warning signs — new cracks, leaning poles, jamming doors, fresh seepage — and engineered upgrading or dignified relocation for settlements already on hazardous slopes.
